# Aesthetics Korea

> The independent guide to skin and aesthetic treatments in South Korea. Independent, source-backed reference on skin treatments in South Korea, from lasers and skin tightening to injectables and skin boosters, and on visiting a Korean skin clinic as an international patient.

Every page answers one question, opens with a short answer, and lists typed sources. A page describing a medical procedure says in its byline whether a clinician has individually reviewed it, and names them only if one has; a page relaying an official Korean rule cites the ministry, agency or statute instead. Not medical advice; not a clinic.

## Skin treatments

- [Botox in South Korea: anti-wrinkle injections and the Korean brands](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/botox/): Botulinum toxin relaxes the muscle making a line. How it works, how long it lasts, and the Korean rule that every batch is released by the government.
- [Chemical skin peels: the cheap agent that beat the aggressive one](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/chemical-peel/): In pooled melasma trials in darker skin, glycolic acid outperformed trichloroacetic acid. And the maintenance topicals matter more than the peel itself.
- [Dermal filler in South Korea: what face filler is and what it does](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/dermal-filler/): Filler adds volume where it is injected. What hyaluronic acid filler is, what it can and cannot do, how long it lasts, and the one risk worth understanding.
- [Exosome skin treatments: promising evidence, and a regulatory question](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/exosome/): The published human studies are small and positive. The more urgent question in South Korea is whether the product being injected is licensed as a drug at all.
- [Face slimming injections: two licensed products, and everything else](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/fat-dissolving-injection/): South Korea's health technology agency reviewed 38 studies and could not confirm long-term effect. Only two submental fat injections are licensed here.
- [Fractional laser skin resurfacing: ablative or not, the trials tied](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/fractional-laser/): Pooled trials found no difference between ablative and non-ablative fractional lasers — on results or on pigmentation risk. Downtime is what changes.
- [InMode skin tightening is a platform, not one treatment](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/inmode/): Forma, FaceTite and Morpheus8 are different procedures on one system, and one of them goes under the skin. What each does and why the distinction matters.
- [Juvelook (PDLLA) skin booster: a collagen stimulator, not a filler](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/juvelook/): PDLLA provokes your own collagen, so it is slow and not reversible like hyaluronic acid. Its one trial tested a sister product, Juvelook Volume.
- [Laser toning for melasma: the cheaper skin laser that outperformed](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/laser-toning/): Laser toning outperformed pico lasers for melasma in pooled trials. But roughly 10% of East Asian patients develop mottled hypopigmentation that lasts years.
- [Pico laser for dark spots: what the pooled trials found](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/pico-laser/): Picosecond lasers are sold as the newer, better option for pigmentation. For melasma, a 2026 meta-analysis of 52 trials found they did not beat controls.
- [Potenza RF microneedling: which skin problems it treats well](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/potenza/): Needles carry radiofrequency past the epidermis. A 2026 review of 41 studies found credible efficacy for acne scars and safety across skin types in trials.
- [Radiesse collagen filler: what is licensed, what is hyperdiluted, what cannot be undone](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/radiesse/): Radiesse fills and stimulates collagen, and no enzyme dissolves it. The hyperdiluted version sold as a skin booster has no randomised trials behind it.
- [Rejuran, the salmon DNA skin booster: what the evidence shows](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/rejuran/): A Korean polynucleotide injectable marketed for skin quality. What it is, and what a 2024 systematic review found when it pooled the trials.
- [Sculptra collagen injections: lasting volume, and the nodule question](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/sculptra/): Poly-L-lactic acid builds volume over months and lasts years. Published nodule rates run from 1.2% to 41%, and dilution volume is what moves them.
- [Skin booster injections: what the category means and what trials show](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/skin-booster/): An umbrella term, not one treatment. What is actually injected, what controlled trials measured, and how to read a 97% efficacy figure.
- [Thermage skin tightening: what monopolar radiofrequency depth buys you](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/thermage-flx/): Monopolar radiofrequency heats deep and diffusely to contract collagen. How it differs from the other RF devices Korean clinics sell, and what trials report.
- [Face thread lift in South Korea: what it is and how long it lasts](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/thread-lift/): Barbed threads pulled under the skin to lift sagging tissue. How it works, what the published follow-up shows about duration, and how often complications occur.
- [Ultherapy and Korean HIFU skin tightening: what the ultrasound does](https://aestheticskorea.com/treatments/ultherapy/): Focused ultrasound heats tissue deep enough to reach the SMAS. What the pooled evidence shows, how Shurink relates to it, and what it will not do.

## Skin concerns

- [Acne scars: what South Korean clinics use, and what the evidence supports](https://aestheticskorea.com/concerns/acne-scars/): Atrophic scars need remodelling, not resurfacing alone. What South Korean clinics offer, what the pooled evidence shows, and why skin type decides.
- [Enlarged pores and pore treatments: the thinnest evidence on this site](https://aestheticskorea.com/concerns/enlarged-pores/): The whole evidence base for pores is 19 trials and 591 people. Pores cannot be closed — what treatment changes is how visible they are.
- [Glass skin: what it actually means, and what produces it](https://aestheticskorea.com/concerns/glass-skin/): Dermatology now has a working definition of glow, and it is about even reflectance rather than shine. What that means for what you book in Korea.
- [Is laser safe for darker skin? The evidence, and what it means in South Korea](https://aestheticskorea.com/concerns/laser-on-darker-skin/): Higher Fitzpatrick types carry a real risk of hyperpigmentation and mottled pigment loss after laser. What the studies show, and what to settle first.
- [Pigmentation and dark spots: four problems that share one word](https://aestheticskorea.com/concerns/pigmentation/): Four different problems get called pigmentation, and they need different treatment. The best-evidenced melasma option is a tablet plus a cream, not a laser.
- [Sagging skin: tightening, repositioning, and telling them apart](https://aestheticskorea.com/concerns/sagging-skin/): Most non-surgical lifting does not lift. Which treatments tighten skin in place, which move tissue that has descended, and what the pooled evidence supports.
- [Skin quality: four categories, and why most packages only treat one](https://aestheticskorea.com/concerns/skin-texture/): Skin quality has a consensus definition — tone evenness, surface evenness, firmness, glow. Most packages target one of the four and are sold as improving all.
- [Wrinkles and fine lines: which lines move, which stay, and what each answers to](https://aestheticskorea.com/concerns/wrinkles/): Toxin works on movement lines, tretinoin on photodamage, and daily sunscreen stopped detectable aging over 4.5 years. Different lines need different tools.

## Comparisons

- [Rejuran vs Juvelook: two different bets on your own collagen](https://aestheticskorea.com/compare/rejuran-vs-juvelook/): Both are injected for skin quality — one salmon-derived polynucleotide, one a lactic acid polymer. Neither can be dissolved, and neither is well evidenced.
- [Thermage vs Ultherapy: heat spread wide, or focused deep](https://aestheticskorea.com/compare/thermage-vs-ultherapy/): Two ways of heating tissue to tighten it. What separates them is depth and how the energy is delivered — and neither repositions tissue that has descended.
- [Ultherapy vs Shurink: what the records show, and what no study shows](https://aestheticskorea.com/compare/ultherapy-vs-shurink/): Two ultrasound lifting devices, one documented difference, and no head-to-head trial. What the regulatory records say before you accept a substitution.

## Costs

- [Rejuran price in Seoul: what 11 clinics charged in November 2026](https://aestheticskorea.com/cost/rejuran-cost-korea/): Rejuran Healer 2 cc cost ₩165,000 to ₩319,000 including VAT at 11 Seoul clinics in November 2026. What the price covers and what changes it.
- [Skin treatment prices in Seoul, November 2026: botox to Thermage](https://aestheticskorea.com/cost/seoul-skin-treatment-prices/): What Seoul clinics charged for botox, filler, skin boosters, Ultherapy, Thermage, Shurink, Potenza and toning in November 2026, 10 to 15 clinics each.

## Visit Guide

- [After you fly home: aftercare, follow-up, and who to contact](https://aestheticskorea.com/visit/after-you-fly-home/): What to leave South Korea holding, who to contact from abroad, and the statutory route that exists if a complication becomes a dispute.
- [Booking a skin clinic in South Korea: what to settle first](https://aestheticskorea.com/visit/before-you-book/): What you actually need to be treated, who will interpret, what to get in writing before you pay a deposit, and what to do once you have flown home.
- [Flying after a skin treatment: what actually restricts you](https://aestheticskorea.com/visit/flying-after-treatment/): Aviation waiting periods exist for trapped gas and do not cover lasers or injectables. Your clinic's interval and follow-up plan are what apply.
- [How to look for a skin clinic in South Korea](https://aestheticskorea.com/visit/how-to-find-a-clinic/): Not which clinic — how to search. Where Koreans look, what a clinic's name says about its doctor, and the claims the profession calls unlawful.
- [More than one treatment in one trip: what can share a visit](https://aestheticskorea.com/visit/more-than-one-treatment/): Combinations are normal and studied. What the consensus says can be done in one session, what needs a gap, and what a short trip cannot compress.
- [Taking medicine and skincare home from South Korea](https://aestheticskorea.com/visit/taking-medicine-home/): Leaving Korea is rarely the problem. The rule that decides is where you land, and Japan allows 24 cosmetics per item, or 120 if under 60 mL.

## Official Resources

- [What Korean law says about brokers, referral fees and clinic ads](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/brokers-referrals-and-clinic-advertising/): South Korea's Medical Service Act bars introducing, referring or soliciting patients for profit. What that means for agencies offering to book your treatment.
- [How to check whether a device or injectable is approved in South Korea](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/check-device-and-drug-approval/): South Korea's regulator publishes what it has approved. How to look up a laser, device or injectable before you agree to it, and what approval does not mean.
- [What a Korean clinic must post about its prices — and cannot exceed](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/clinic-price-disclosure/): Korean law makes a clinic display its non-covered prices, bars it from charging more than the posted amount, and makes it report those prices to the government.
- [Is your Korean clinic registered to treat foreign patients?](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/clinic-registration-foreign-patients/): Korean law requires clinics and agencies to register before treating foreign patients. How the register works, and how to check a clinic against it.
- [K-ETA in 2026: who is exempt, and who still needs one](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/k-eta/): Exempt to 31 December 2026: Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia and more. Thailand and Malaysia are visa-free but still need K-ETA.
- [KAHF accreditation: the tier above registration in South Korea](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/kahf-accreditation/): Registration lets a Korean clinic treat foreign patients. KAHF is the stricter tier above it, assessed on patient safety as well as service.
- [If a Korean clinic goes wrong: the official dispute route](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/medical-dispute-mediation/): South Korea has a statutory agency that mediates medical disputes outside the courts. What it can do, what it costs, and how a patient reaches it.
- [Your medical records in South Korea: the right, and what it costs](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/medical-records-access/): You can require a Korean clinic to hand over your own records. What the statute says, what to ask for, and the ceilings the ministry sets on the fees.
- [South Korea's medical visas: C-3-3 and G-1-10](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/medical-visa/): South Korea has two visa categories for foreign patients. Who they are for, how long they last, and why only a registered clinic or agency can invite you.
- [South Korea's VAT refund on cosmetic procedures ended on 1 January 2026](https://aestheticskorea.com/official/vat-refund-cosmetic-procedures/): The 10% VAT refund for foreign patients having cosmetic procedures in South Korea applied to services supplied up to 31 December 2025. It was not extended.

## Glossary

Official terms and the everyday words for them, at https://aestheticskorea.com/glossary/. "Skin treatment" on this site means an aesthetic procedure done in a medical clinic.

- Aesthetic procedure (also: skin treatment, cosmetic treatment, beauty treatment): A procedure done in a medical clinic to change how skin or the face looks, rather than to treat a disease: lasers, energy devices, injections and peels. This is what the industry calls aesthetic medicine.
- Dermatology clinic (피부과) (also: skin clinic, derm clinic, Korean skin clinic): The kind of clinic where most of the procedures on this site are done in South Korea. Patients use the Korean word 피부과 for both medical and cosmetic visits.
- Aesthetic concern (also: skin concern, skin problem, skin issue): What a patient wants changed, such as pigmentation, acne scars, pores or sagging. Pages under Skin concerns start from the concern and lead to the treatments used for it.
- Energy-based device (also: skin laser, lifting laser, skin tightening machine, HIFU, RF): A machine that heats tissue with light, radiofrequency or focused ultrasound. Patients often call all of them lasers.
- Non-surgical lifting (also: skin lifting, skin tightening, facelift without surgery): Treatments that tighten skin with heat, or support it with threads, without surgery.
- Injectable (also: skin injection, face injection, beauty injection): Anything injected to change appearance: botulinum toxin, fillers, collagen stimulators and skin boosters. They differ in what they do and in whether they can be reversed, which each treatment page sets out.
- Skin booster (also: skin booster injection, glass skin injection, hydration injection): A marketing label for small injections spread across an area to improve skin quality rather than add volume. It names a technique, not a product, and products sold under it contain different actives.
- Botulinum toxin (also: botox, anti-wrinkle injection, jaw botox, skin botox): A muscle-relaxing injection. Botox is one brand of it; Korean brands are sold under their own names.
- Dermal filler (also: filler, face filler, lip filler): A gel injected to add volume or shape. The filler page covers what it is made of and which kinds can be dissolved.
- Hyperpigmentation (also: dark spots, brown spots, uneven skin tone, melasma): Patches of skin darker than the skin around them.
- Recovery period (also: downtime, healing time): The days after a procedure when redness, swelling or bruising may be visible. Each treatment page lists it under Downtime in its key facts.
- Foreign patient (외국인환자) (also: medical tourist, skin trip to Korea, beauty trip to Korea): Someone travelling to South Korea for treatment. Korean law uses the term foreign patient, and the official pages explain the registration and visa rules that come with it.

## Approval status

Whether 55 products used in Korean clinics are registered in Korea (MFDS), the US (FDA), Australia (TGA) and Japan (PMDA), with record numbers, at https://aestheticskorea.com/official/approval-status/. Data: https://aestheticskorea.com/data/approvals/approval-status-2026-11.csv. "Not found" means searched and not found, not banned.

## Korean clinic names

Names used on Korean clinic price lists, with what each is and its English names, at https://aestheticskorea.com/glossary/korean-clinic-names/.

- 스킨보톡스 (seukin botokseu, skin botox, microbotox, mesobotox, microdroplet botulinum toxin, intradermal botulinum toxin): Botulinum toxin injected as many tiny droplets into the skin (intradermal) instead of into the muscle. Price lists sell it by area or by cc of diluted solution (e.g. full face 2cc), not by units, and the toxin brand varies by option.
- 사각턱보톡스 (턱보톡스) (sagakteok botokseu (teok botokseu), masseter botox, jaw botox, jawline slimming botox): Botulinum toxin injected into the masseter (jaw-closing) muscle to slim the lower-face contour. Priced by units (e.g. 50U, 100U). Nabota's Korean label includes marked benign masseter hypertrophy; the other toxin labels checked here do not list it.
- 승모근보톡스 (seungmogeun botokseu, trapezius botox, shoulder botox, trap botox): Botulinum toxin injected into the upper trapezius muscle for shoulder and neck-line contouring. Listed as body botox priced by units (often 100U), sometimes bundled with calf botox.
- 눈앞개봉 (nunap gaebong, opened in front of you, unsealed in your presence): Clinic promise to open a new, sealed product box in front of the patient before the treatment. A clinic's own promise, not a regulated certification; some clinics do it only on request at booking.
- 정품팁 (jeongpum tip, genuine tip, authentic tip, original cartridge): Clinic phrase saying a device treatment uses the manufacturer's genuine tip or cartridge (e.g. Ultherapy, Thermage, Oligio). Often paired with a promise that the shot count is shown to the patient; it is the clinic's claim, not an outside check.
- 정품 / 정품정량 (jeongpum / jeongpum jeongnyang, genuine product, genuine product, full dose): Clinic claim that the product is genuine (정품) and used at the stated dose (정량). Appears on most toxin listings; it is the clinic's own claim, not an MFDS certification.
- 수면 (sumyeon, sedation, IV sedation, sleep anaesthesia): Short for sedation (수면마취) offered with a procedure, as in 수면 울쎄라 (Ultherapy under sedation). Whether the sedation fee is in the listed price varies: some listings say anaesthesia is included, others ask you to request sedation when booking.
- 체험가 (cheheomga, trial price, intro price): Trial price: a discounted introductory price, usually limited to one use per person and one area. Conditions such as 1인 1회 (once per person) and no stacking with other offers apply; the regular price is listed beside it.
- 첫방문가 (첫방문) (cheotbangmunga (cheotbangmun), first-visit price, new-patient price): First-visit price: a discount only for a patient's first visit to that clinic, usually once. Often combined with 체험가; later visits are charged at the regular listed price.
- 부가세 별도 (bugase byeoldo, VAT excluded, plus VAT, excl. VAT): Price shown excludes VAT, which is added on top; Korean VAT law takes cosmetic procedures out of the medical-service VAT exemption. Clinic websites may quote VAT-excluded prices while booking-app listings show VAT-included prices (VAT 포함), so compare like with like. The decree lists items such as wrinkle removal, skin regeneration and fat dissolution; toxin is not named by itself.
- 국산 보톡스 (guksan botokseu, Korean-made botox, domestic toxin): Botulinum toxin type A made by a Korean company, such as Botulax, Nabota, Meditoxin, Coretox or Liztox. Listings use 보톡스 generically, so 국산 보톡스 is not Allergan BOTOX; ask for the brand name.
- 수입 보톡스 (suip botokseu, imported botox, imported toxin): Botulinum toxin type A made abroad and imported, such as Allergan BOTOX, Merz Xeomin or Ipsen Dysport. Usually priced higher than 국산 options on the same listing; listings name the brand next to 수입.
- 정제 톡신 (정제형) (jeongje toksin (jeongjehyeong), purified toxin, pure toxin): Clinic term for toxins sold as the 150 kDa neurotoxin without complexing proteins, such as Xeomin and Coretox. 정제 is a marketing word, not an MFDS category; MFDS records list both products as 클로스트리디움 보툴리눔 독소 A형(150kDa).
- 물광주사 (mulgwang jusa, water-glow injection, glass-skin injection, hyaluronic acid skin booster): No fixed product: a clinic name for skin injections of a hyaluronic-acid skin booster, sold by cc. Brand differs by clinic and is sometimes named on the listing; some clinics mix in skin botox (물광톡스).
- 윤곽주사 (yungwak jusa, contour injection, V-line injection): No fixed product: a clinic name for face-contouring injections of fat-dissolving mixtures, often under the clinic's own name (e.g. 브이핏, 엔V). Mixtures vary by clinic and are often not disclosed; listings offer steroid-included and steroid-free versions, so ask what is in it.
- 지방분해주사 (jibang bunhae jusa, fat-dissolving injection, lipolysis injection, fat-melting injection): No fixed product: a clinic name for fat-dissolving injections; the MFDS-approved product of this type is Vyolet (deoxycholic acid) for submental fat. Most clinic 지방분해주사 are house mixtures, not Vyolet; steroid-free versions are labelled 스테로이드 불포함.
- 백옥주사 (baegok jusa, glutathione injection, glutathione drip): Glutathione injection, given by injection or IV drip at clinics; its MFDS-approved uses are liver-function and chemotherapy indications, not skin whitening. MFDS describes the cosmetic use as off-label (허가 외 사용); it is a prescription-only medicine.
- 신데렐라주사 (sinderella jusa, Cinderella injection, thioctic acid injection): Thioctic acid (alpha-lipoic acid) given by IV injection; its approved uses in Korea are medical, not cosmetic. MFDS describes the cosmetic use as off-label; MFDS says it is for IV use only.
- 마늘주사 (maneul jusa, garlic injection, fursultiamine injection, vitamin B1 injection): Fursultiamine (a vitamin B1-like compound) injection, given IV, under the skin or into muscle. It contains no garlic; MFDS lists it among injections used outside approved uses for cosmetic purposes.
- 감초주사 (gamcho jusa, licorice injection, glycyrrhizin injection): Glycyrrhizic acid combination injection (with glycine and cysteine), given IV. Its approved uses in Korea are medical, not cosmetic; MFDS lists it among injections used outside approved uses for cosmetic purposes.
- 태반주사 (taeban jusa, placenta injection): Injection containing human placenta extract or hydrolysate (자하거추출물/가수분해물). MFDS lists it among injections used outside approved uses for cosmetic purposes.
- 보톡스 (botokseu, Botox, BOTOX, botulinum toxin): Used two ways: AbbVie/Allergan's BOTOX brand (보톡스주), and the everyday word for any botulinum toxin injection. Listings say 국산 보톡스 for Korean brands; Allergan's own product is usually labelled 엘러간 or 수입 엘러간.
- 보툴렉스 (botullekseu, Botulax): Hugel's botulinum toxin type A injection (보툴렉스주), approved by MFDS in 2009. MFDS lists 50, 100, 150, 200 and 300 unit versions.
- 나보타 (nabota, Nabota): Daewoong Pharmaceutical's botulinum toxin type A injection (나보타주), approved by MFDS in 2013. Its Korean label includes temporary improvement of marked benign masseter hypertrophy.
- 메디톡신 (meditoksin, Meditoxin, Neuronox (export name)): Medytox's botulinum toxin type A injection (메디톡신주), approved by MFDS in 2006. Contains human serum albumin; Medytox's albumin-free 150 kDa product is a separate brand, Coretox.
- 코어톡스 (koeotokseu, Coretox): Medytox's 150 kDa botulinum toxin type A injection without human serum albumin (코어톡스주), approved by MFDS in 2016. Listed as 국산 and often marketed as a 정제 (purified) toxin.
- 제오민 (jeomin, Xeomin): Merz's 150 kDa botulinum toxin type A injection (제오민주), made by Merz Pharma and IDT Biologika in Germany and approved by MFDS in 2009. Listed as 수입 and often marketed as a 정제 (purified) toxin.
- 디스포트 (diseupoteu, Dysport): Ipsen's botulinum toxin type A-haemagglutinin complex injection (디스포트주), approved by MFDS in 1999. Comes as a 500-unit vial; contains human serum albumin and lactose.
- 리즈톡스 (rijeutokseu, Liztox, Hutox (export name)): Huons BioPharma's botulinum toxin type A injection (리즈톡스주), approved by MFDS in 2016. Listed as 국산.
- 제테마더톡신 (더톡신) (jetema deotoksin (deotoksin), JETEMA The Toxin): JETEMA's botulinum toxin type A injection (제테마더톡신주) for the Korean market, approved by MFDS in 2024. An earlier 100U product approved in 2020 is export-only (수출용).
- 뉴럭스 (nyureokseu, Newlux): Numeco's botulinum toxin type A injection (뉴럭스주), made under contract by Medytox and approved by MFDS in 2023. Listed as 국산.
- 연어주사 (yeoneo jusa, salmon injection): No fixed product: a clinic nickname ("salmon injection") for injections of salmon-derived DNA ingredients, which can mean either a PDRN prescription drug or a PN skin booster such as Rejuran. One name covers two ingredient classes: PDRN injections registered by MFDS as prescription drugs (e.g. 뉴클레오주) and PN skin boosters (e.g. 리쥬란 힐러, 리쥬란 HB). Ask which product and how many cc before comparing prices.
- 리쥬란 힐러 (rijyuran hilleo, Rejuran Healer, Rejuran): PharmaResearch's original Rejuran injectable, made of polynucleotide (PN) derived from salmon DNA. Often just called 리쥬란. Some clinic price lists also file it under 연어주사.
- 리쥬란 HB (rijyuran HB, Rejuran HB): A Rejuran product that combines polynucleotide (PN) with hyaluronic acid. Clinics also list 리쥬란HB+ or 리쥬란 HB plus; whether the Plus version differs in composition was not confirmed from a maker or MFDS source.
- 엑소좀 (eksojom, exosome): No fixed product: a clinic term for treatments that use an exosome-containing solution, often applied after microneedling (MTS) or RF microneedling rather than a single named product. MFDS press release of 2023-01-05 is titled 'injection into the skin is only possible with drugs and medical devices'. Ask the clinic for the product name and whether it is applied on the skin or injected.
- 쥬베룩 (jyuberuk, Juvelook): VAIM's Juvelook, an injectable combining poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) 42.5 mg with hyaluronic acid 7.5 mg per vial. 쥬베룩 볼륨 is a separate, higher-dose product; check which one a price refers to.
- 쥬베룩 스킨 (jyuberuk seukin, Juvelook): Clinic listing name for Juvelook used as a skin booster (also written 쥬베룩스킨 or 쥬베룩 스킨부스터). Not the same as 쥬베룩 볼륨. Clinics price it by cc or by part of a vial.
- 쥬베룩 볼륨 (jyuberuk bollyum, Juvelook Volume, Lenisna): VAIM's Juvelook Volume (formerly Lenisna), a separate product combining PDLLA 170 mg with hyaluronic acid 30 mg per vial. Separate product from 쥬베룩 / 쥬베룩 스킨. Price lists use both cc and whole vial (한병) units, so compare per unit.
- 스킨바이브 (seukinbaibeu, SKINVIVE, SKINVIVE by JUVÉDERM): Allergan's SKINVIVE by JUVÉDERM, a hyaluronic acid microdroplet injectable for the skin. Part of the Juvéderm brand family but a separate product from Juvéderm fillers.
- 샤넬주사 (syanel jusa, Chanel injection): No fixed product: a clinic nickname for a premium skin-booster glow injection; it is not a Chanel product and the product used varies by clinic. One clinic describes it as an umbrella term for premium HA glow brands. Ask for the actual product name before comparing prices.
- 스컬트라 (seukeolteura, Sculptra): Galderma's Sculptra, an injectable biostimulator containing poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) microparticles. Usually priced per vial (한병) rather than per cc.
- 레디어스 (redieoseu, Radiesse): Merz's Radiesse, an injectable containing calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA) particles. Also spelled 래디어스; both spellings can appear on one page. Some clinics also sell it diluted as a skin booster (레디어스 스킨부스터).
- 래디어스 (raedieoseu, Radiesse): Alternative spelling of 레디어스: Merz's Radiesse, an injectable containing calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA) particles. Same product as 레디어스. Diluted skin-booster use is priced differently from a full vial.
- 엘란쎄 (ellansse, Ellansé): Ellansé, an injectable of polycaprolactone (PCL) microspheres in a carboxymethylcellulose gel carrier, made in several versions (S, M, L, E). Price depends on the version and the number of syringes; check which version is quoted.
- 필러 (pilleo, dermal filler, filler): No fixed product: the general word for an injectable dermal filler; on Korean price lists it most often means a hyaluronic acid (HA) filler, priced by brand. The same area can cost several times more depending on brand (e.g. 뉴라미스 vs 벨로테로 vs 쥬비덤/레스틸렌 on one price list). Ask which brand. Collagen stimulators such as 레디어스 or 엘란쎄 are sometimes also called 필러.
- 쥬비덤 (jyubideom, JUVÉDERM, Juvederm): Allergan's JUVÉDERM, a collection of hyaluronic acid dermal fillers. A brand family with several products (e.g. Voluma, Volbella); 스킨바이브 is a separate product in the same family.
- 레스틸렌 (reseutillen, Restylane): Galderma's Restylane, a range of hyaluronic acid fillers (the range also includes Restylane Skinboosters). A brand family; clinics may name a specific product (e.g. 레스틸렌 키스 for Restylane Kysse).
- 벨로테로 (bellotero, BELOTERO, Belotero): Merz's BELOTERO, a hyaluronic acid filler brand. A brand family with several products; ask which one is quoted.
- 뉴라미스 (nyuramiseu, Neuramis): Neuramis, a Korean hyaluronic acid filler brand; the published trial of Neuramis Volume Lidocaine was funded by Medytox. Often priced well below imported HA brands on the same price list.
- 울쎄라 (ulssera, Ultherapy, Ulthera): Ultherapy, a micro-focused ultrasound device with real-time imaging, marketed by Merz Aesthetics. Merz says it is moving from the original Ultherapy device to Ultherapy PRIME; listings that just say 울쎄라 may mean either device.
- 울쎄라피 프라임 (ulsserapi peuraim, Ultherapy PRIME): Ultherapy PRIME, Merz Aesthetics' newer Ultherapy device using micro-focused ultrasound with real-time imaging. A newer generation of the same Merz device line, not a different treatment type; listings show it as a separate item from plain 울쎄라.
- 슈링크 (syuringkeu, Shurink, Ultraformer III): Shurink, the Korean-market name for Classys' HIFU (focused ultrasound) device sold abroad as Ultraformer III. A different product from Ultherapy, made by Classys; same energy type (focused ultrasound) but not the same device.
- 슈링크 유니버스 (syuringkeu yunibeoseu, Shurink Universe, Ultraformer MPT): Shurink Universe, Classys' newer HIFU device, sold outside Korea as Ultraformer MPT. Newer model than 슈링크; Classys' Korean page lists it as a 비침습적 집속형 초음파 (HIFU) device, MFDS permit 제인 21-831호. Not Ultherapy.
- 써마지 (sseomaji, Thermage): Thermage, Solta Medical's monopolar radiofrequency skin-tightening platform; the current model is Thermage FLX. Solta describes FLX as the fourth generation of the Thermage platform, so a listing that only says 써마지 does not state which generation is used; ask.
- 써마지 FLX (sseomaji FLX, Thermage FLX): Thermage FLX, the fourth-generation monopolar radiofrequency device in Solta Medical's Thermage line. Listings often add 4세대 (fourth generation) and a shot count such as 600샷.
- 인모드 포마 (inmodeu poma, InMode Forma, Forma): Forma, an InMode bipolar radiofrequency handpiece that heats the dermis and the layer beneath it. 인모드 alone names the company platform, not one treatment; Forma and FX are different handpieces and are often sold together as 인모드 리프팅.
- 인모드 FX (inmodeu FX, InMode FX, BodyFX, MiniFX): A treatment on InMode's FX family of vacuum bipolar radiofrequency applicators (BodyFX for larger areas, MiniFX for small areas). Korean listings say only FX; which FX handpiece a clinic uses (MiniFX or BodyFX) is not shown on the listing.
- 볼뉴머 (bollyumeo, Volnewmer): Volnewmer, a Classys 6.78 MHz monopolar radiofrequency device. A different product from Thermage, same energy type (monopolar RF); MFDS permit 제허 22-512 호 per Classys.
- 올리지오 (ollijio, Oligio, Oligio X): Oligio, a radiofrequency therapy system made by Wontech of Korea. A different product from Thermage; Oligio X is a later model with its own US clearance.
- 덴서티 (denseoti, Density): Density, a Jeisys Medical device that delivers monopolar and bipolar 6.78 MHz radiofrequency energy into the dermis. A different product from Thermage; made by Jeisys, the Potenza maker.
- 온다리프팅 (ondaripeuting, ONDA, ONDA PRO, Coolwaves): A treatment on ONDA, DEKA's device that uses 2.45 GHz microwave energy (Coolwaves). unni.app files it under 극초단파리프팅 (microwave lifting), separate from ultrasound and RF lifting.
- 리프팅 (ripeuting, lifting): No fixed product: a catch-all listing word for lifting treatments, covering ultrasound, radiofrequency, microwave and laser devices as well as threads. unni.app splits 리프팅 into 초음파 (울쎄라, 슈링크), 고주파 (써마지, 인모드), 극초단파 (온다) and 레이저 (티타늄) groups plus 실리프팅; always check which device is meant.
- 실리프팅 (sillipeuting, thread lift): Thread lift: absorbable or non-absorbable threads placed under the skin, most often PDO threads with cogs. The thread material and brand vary by clinic (PDO, PLLA, PCL and others); the name alone does not tell you which.
- 코그실 / PDO실 (kogeusil / PDO sil, cog thread, barbed thread, PDO thread): 코그실 is a cog (barbed) thread with projections along its length; PDO실 is a thread made of polydioxanone, an absorbable material. The two words describe different things: PDO is the material, cog is the shape. A PDO thread can be smooth (mono) or cogged.
- 레이저토닝 (reijeotoning, laser toning, low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG): A technique, not a device: repeated passes of a large-spot, low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG laser. Sold on many different laser platforms; the listing name does not tell you which machine is used.
- 피코토닝 (pikotoning, pico toning, picosecond laser toning): Laser toning done with a low-fluence picosecond laser (for example a 1064 nm picosecond Nd:YAG) instead of a Q-switched one. A technique name; the picosecond device behind it varies (PicoSure, PicoPlus and others).
- 듀얼토닝 (dyueoltoning, dual toning): A combined toning session: a low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG pass followed straight away by a long-pulse or micropulse Nd:YAG pass. The term is in Korean dermatology papers, but clinics also use 듀얼토닝 for other two-laser pairings (e.g. 엑셀V + 제네시스), so the pairing varies.
- 제네시스토닝 (jenesiseutoning, Laser Genesis): Laser Genesis, Cutera's treatment using a non-ablative 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser, delivered on Cutera's xeo+, excel V+ and excel HR. Listings pair 제네시스 with 엑셀V and other lasers; the listing does not prove a Cutera machine is used.
- 엑셀V (eksel V, excel V, excel V+): excel V / excel V+, a Cutera laser platform; the excel V+ has a 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser that delivers Laser Genesis. Often sold together with 제네시스 or as part of a 듀얼토닝 package.
- 레블라이트 (rebeullaiteu, RevLite SI, RevLite): RevLite SI, a Q-switched Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm and 532 nm) from Cynosure Lutronic, based on ConBio technology. A machine often used for 레이저토닝; the brand name alone is not a treatment.
- 헬리오스 (hellioseu, Helios, Helios III): Helios, a Q-switched Nd:YAG laser line made by Laseroptek of Korea (Helios II, III and later models). The model generation (II, III, IV/785) is rarely stated on listings.
- 피코슈어 (pikosyueo, PicoSure, PicoSure Pro): PicoSure / PicoSure Pro, Cynosure Lutronic's 755 nm picosecond laser, with optional 532 nm and 1064 nm. Listings write 피코슈어 PRO or 피코슈어프로 for the newer model.
- 피코플러스 (pikopeulleoseu, PICOPLUS, PicoPlus): PicoPlus, a Lutronic picosecond laser system cleared in the US at 1064 nm and 532 nm. Some markets sell extra 595/660 nm handpieces; which ones a clinic has varies.
- 포텐자 (potenja, Potenza): Potenza, a Jeisys Medical device that delivers radiofrequency energy through needle tips (invasive mode) or non-needle tips. The tip used changes the treatment; listings name tips such as 모공팁, N팁, 펌핑팁 or CP팁.
- 모공팁 / N팁 (mogongtip / N-tip, Potenza N tip (N-16, N-25, N-49)): Potenza needle tips: N팁 is Jeisys' N-series (N-16, N-25, N-49) non-insulated multi-needle tip; 모공팁 ("pore tip") is a clinic label, not a maker tip name. Jeisys has no tip called a pore tip; it lists pores as a use of its S-series tips, and one listing sells "N팁 모공모드". Ask which tip 모공팁 means.
- 프락셀 (peuraksel, Fraxel, fractional laser): Fraxel is Solta Medical's fractional laser brand, but 프락셀 on Korean listings is used for fractional treatment on many devices. Listings say 피코프락셀, 에어프락셀, 모자이크 3D 프락셀 and 모공프락셀, which are not Solta's Fraxel; ask which machine is used.
- 필링 (pilling, chemical peel, peel): Usually a chemical peel: a solution (often an alpha- or beta-hydroxy acid) applied to the skin to exfoliate it, at superficial, medium or deep depth. Listings also use -필 for many house-named skin-care steps (아쿠아필, 라라필, 블랙필) that are not all chemical peels.
- 아쿠아필 (akuapil, Aqua Peel, hydradermabrasion): No fixed product: a water-based exfoliation (hydradermabrasion) facial; Classys' AQUAPURE device has a handpiece called AQUAPEEL. Usually sold as a low-cost skin-care step or a 체험가 add-on; the device behind it is rarely named.
- 모델링팩 (modellingpaek, modeling mask): No fixed product: a face mask added at the end of a skin-care or laser package. Listings sell it as an add-on (e.g. 피코토닝 & 모델링팩) and do not name the mask product.
- 크라이오 (keuraio, cryo): No fixed product: a skin-care add-on sold under the word cryo ("cold"), usually paired with 진정관리 (soothing care) after another treatment. Not the same as cryolipolysis (fat freezing); listings do not name a device, so ask what is used.
